facts.title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
facts.event_hint: Research paper presents KAP (Knowledge Access Planning), a paradigm-shifting execution abstraction for LLM serving that bridges the gap between structured knowledge priors and runtime KV consumption
facts.problem: The Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: modern LLM systems produce high-value structured priors (ranked evidence, graph topology, multimodal alignment, confidence signals) but LLM serving backends observe only flat token sequences after prompt serialization, forcing dense and uniform consumption of full KV state during decoding. This increases latency and degrades throughput even when reasoning depends on only a small fraction of context
facts.mechanism: KAP elevates structured knowledge priors from passive prompt-construction hints into first-class physical execution artifacts through a universal intermediate representation - the runtime access plan - which compiles structured knowledge signals to govern physical KV access without altering logical prompt semantics, model weights, or training procedures. Instantiated as GraphSpec compiler-executor connecting Graph-RAG knowledge selection to vLLM serving backend, shifting LLM serving from token-aware context consumption to plan-driven, knowledge-aware runtime consumption

evidence.claim: GraphSpec reduces proposal-time KV access to 5.5% of source KV state at 128K context length
evidence.condition: 128K context length, long-context QA workload on SPIQA dataset
evidence.source_locator: Abstract, PDF Page 1

evidence.claim: GraphSpec achieves 1.08x-1.19x decode throughput speedup over full-context baseline across 4K-128K context lengths
evidence.baseline: Full-context decoding with standard vLLM backend
evidence.condition: SPIQA dataset, 4K-128K context lengths, decode throughput (TPS) measurement
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 13, Table 2

evidence.claim: GraphSpec Top-3 tolerant acceptance rate remains high (0.953-0.962) across all context lengths, indicating proposal effectiveness
evidence.condition: 4K-128K context lengths, Top-3 tolerant proposal acceptance rate metric
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 13, Table 2

evidence.claim: GraphSpec maintains answer quality comparable to full-context decoding, with pass rates differing by at most 1.9 percentage points at 64K (87.9% vs 86.0%)
evidence.condition: 64K context length, LLM similarity pass rate with 0.5 threshold
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 13, Table 3

evidence.claim: Physical concat (prompt materialization without runtime access plan) achieves only 73.9% pass rate vs GraphSpec 87.9% at 64K, proving runtime access plan is essential
evidence.condition: 64K context length, same evidence selected but materialized as shortened prompt
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 14, Table 4

facts.evaluation_context: Evaluated on SPIQA dataset with 4K-128K context lengths using vLLM serving backend. Graph-RAG evidence and priors frozen before benchmarking; frontend retrieval excluded from TTFT measurements. LLM-as-judge quality metric with 0.5 threshold independently validated (95% judge-human agreement on 100 sampled answers). Throughput covers complete executor path, not isolated model-forward performance
facts.limitations: Evaluation validates KAP through GraphSpec, a single concrete instantiation with Graph-RAG frontend and vLLM backend. Results strongest for long-context QA workloads where graph-derived priors can be grounded in evidence spans. Effectiveness depends on quality of knowledge priors, compiler's ability to translate into useful runtime access plans, and backend's ability to execute plans without excessive metadata/synchronization overhead. Other KAP instantiations may use different frontends, compilers, access policies, or backends
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to AI infrastructure horizontal tracking: addresses fundamental architectural mismatch in LLM serving systems, provides concrete system mechanism (runtime access plan IR), demonstrates end-to-end efficiency gains (1.08x-1.19x speedup) with quality preservation. Should be categorized under 'serving_runtime_compiler' direction. Represents paradigm shift from token-aware to knowledge-aware runtime consumption

facts.title: SparseDitto: Customizing GPU Kernels for Different Sparsity Patterns with LLM-Based Agentic System
facts.event_hint: SparseDitto (U. Minnesota / Northeastern) uses LLM agents (GPT-5.6-terra) to auto-generate per-matrix, per-operator, per-GPU sparse kernels, achieving a 2.68x geo-mean speedup over cuSPARSE on an RTX PRO 6000 (max 146.61x) and 2.79x on an H200 (max 78.5x), and accelerating full-batch GCN training by up to 3.39x.
facts.problem: GPU sparse-kernel performance can change by orders of magnitude with the sparsity pattern even when the matrix, operator, library, and GPU are unchanged: for one 355K-nonzeros matrix cuSPARSE completes SpMM in 37 us using CSR but 13 ms using Blocked-ELL — a 350x gap caused solely by representation — and no single implementation consistently dominates across patterns and operators.
facts.mechanism: An LLM-based agentic system that treats the workload as the data: a lightweight additive energy model (15.9K params) ranks established sparse strategies from structural features of the input matrix; an architecture-aware planner proposes several candidate designs; coding and verification agents (all GPT-5.6-terra, reasoning effort low, 8196 tokens/call) implement, compile, benchmark, and refine them using on-target GPU measurements, under one unified framework covering SpMV, SpMM, and SpGEMM, with a single predeclared FP32 correctness bound.

evidence.claim: Across three sparse operators and a diverse set of matrices, SparseDitto achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 2.68x over cuSPARSE on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU (95% CI [2.48, 2.89]), with a maximum of 146.61x; on an NVIDIA H200 GPU it achieves 2.79x (95% CI [2.61, 2.99]), with a maximum of 78.5x.
evidence.condition: Geometric mean over validated tasks; 95% CI by bootstrapping (20,000 resamples of log-speedups); H200 kernels regenerated from scratch on the new target
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 4.1): 'On the RTX PRO 6000, SparseDitto reaches 2.68x over cuSPARSE (95% CI [2.48, 2.89]). On the H200 ... It reaches 2.79x (95% CI [2.61, 2.99]) ...' and PDF Page 1 (Abstract): 'a maximum of 146.61x ... On an NVIDIA H200 GPU, it achieves 2.79x, with a maximum of 78.5x.'

evidence.claim: For one matrix with 355K nonzeros, cuSPARSE completes SpMM in 37 us using CSR but requires 13 ms using Blocked-ELL — a 350x difference caused solely by the representation and its associated kernel, illustrating that a design highly effective for one sparsity pattern can be significantly inefficient for another.
evidence.value: 37 us (CSR) vs 13 ms (Blocked-ELL) = 350x gap on the same SpMM/matrix
evidence.condition: Same matrix (355K nonzeros), same SpMM operator, same GPU; RTX PRO 6000, CUDA 13.0
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Introduction): 'For one matrix with 355 K nonzeros, cuSPARSE completes SpMM in 37 us using CSR but requires 13 ms using Blocked-ELL — a 350x difference caused solely by the representation and its associated kernel.'

evidence.claim: Against cuSPARSE on the RTX PRO 6000, SparseDitto's SpMM speedup is 4.46x at K=8, 2.81x at K=32, 1.92x at K=128, and 1.68x at K=256 — the gain is largest at small dense widths and narrows as K grows; the H200 follows the same trend (4.18x, 2.81x, 1.96x, 1.87x).
evidence.condition: SpMM (sparse x dense), varying dense width K in {8,32,128,256}; RTX PRO 6000 and H200
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 4.1, SpMM): 'Against cuSPARSE, SparseDitto achieves 4.46x at K=8, 2.81x at K=32, 1.92x at K=128, and 1.68x at K=256. The gain is largest at the small dense widths and narrows as K grows. The H200 follows the same trend, at 4.18x, 2.81x, 1.96x, and 1.87x.'

evidence.claim: SparseDitto is 1.57x-5.37x faster than four SOTA specialized systems on matched inputs: against CB-SpMV it is 1.91x/1.57x faster on the two GPUs (CB-SpMV itself reaches only 1.35x/1.70x over cuSPARSE); on the 13 matrices AlphaSparse handles, SparseDitto is 5.34x faster and AlphaSparse reaches only 0.62x over cuSPARSE.
evidence.value: 1.91x/1.57x faster than CB-SpMV; 5.34x faster than AlphaSparse (which is 0.62x vs cuSPARSE)
evidence.condition: Matched inputs/configs; AlphaSparse correct on only 13 matrices under 1800s budget; DTC-SpMM 0.73x (K=8) -> 0.58x (K=256) on Blackwell
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 4.1, SpMV): 'On the same inputs, SparseDitto is 1.91x and 1.57x faster than CB-SpMV ... On the 13 matrices it handles, SparseDitto is 5.34x faster, and AlphaSparse only reaches 0.62x over cuSPARSE.'

evidence.claim: The generated SpMM kernels accelerate full-batch GCN training (2-layer, Reddit) by up to 3.39x at K=8 over cuSPARSE (DTC-SpMM 0.94x at K=8), with each result averaging 100 epochs after 10 warmup and four sparse aggregations per epoch.
evidence.value: GCN epoch up to 3.39x faster (K=8); DTC-SpMM 0.94x at K=8
evidence.condition: 2-layer full-batch GCN on Reddit, unweighted symmetric adjacency, K in {8,32,128,256}, 100 epochs after 10 warmup, 4 sparse aggregations/epoch
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 10-11 (Section 4.6 and Figure 8): 'we evaluate the generated kernels in a two-layer full-batch GCN on Reddit ... Each result averages 100 epochs after 10 warmup epochs ...' Figure 8 labels: '3.39x ... 1.87x ... 1.01x ... 1.14x' and Abstract: 'accelerate full-batch GCN training by up to 3.39x.'

facts.evaluation_context: Operators: SpMV, SpMM (dense width K in {8,32,128,256}), SpGEMM, in a unified framework. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and H200, CUDA 13.0. Baselines: cuSPARSE (primary, FP32 reference), CB-SpMV, AlphaSparse, DTC-SpMM, SparseTIR, HSMU-SpGEMM. Measurement: CUDA events, 5 warmup + 10 timed executions, arithmetic mean, 95% CI by bootstrapping (20,000 resamples). Correctness: |y - y_ref| <= 1e-5 + 1e-3|y_ref| (SpMV/SpMM); exact structure + value bound (SpGEMM). LLM config: GPT-5.6-terra, reasoning effort low, 8196 tokens/call; search budget 3 strategy branches x up to 5 iterations + 5 more for the two fastest. Strategy selector: 15.9K params, 400 SuiteSparse matrices, 600 epochs, ~2s training on one GPU. 127/350 tasks (36%) won by a strategy outside the selector vocabulary.
facts.limitations: Gains narrow sharply at large dense widths (SpMM 4.46x at K=8 down to 1.68x at K=256 on RTX PRO 6000). Seven of the largest matrices trigger a cuSPARSE SpGEMM out-of-resources error and are excluded (no reference). AlphaSparse's released implementation fails on more than half of tested matrices. DTC-SpMM, which reported >1.5x on an RTX 4090, falls below cuSPARSE (0.73x-0.58x) on the Blackwell GPU, showing strong hardware sensitivity of specialized systems. Results depend on a specific LLM (GPT-5.6-terra) and search budget. SparseTIR falls to 0.13-0.20x on the matrix behind the 350x format cliff.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to AI accelerator architecture and GPU kernel generation: demonstrates an LLM-agentic approach that closes the representation-sensitivity gap of sparse GPU kernels (the 350x cuSPARSE format cliff) with a 2.68-2.79x geo-mean speedup and up to 146x on individual matrices across two GPU generations, plus end-to-end GCN training speedups — useful evidence for auto-tuning/specialized-kernel strategies in GPU sparse-compute stacks.
source_notes: Primary source: arXiv:2608.05033v1, Li, Sun, Tang, Wang, Hong, Ding (U. Minnesota / Northeastern), 5 Aug 2026; document.fetch_status=FETCHED.

All speedups are geometric means over validated tasks with 95% bootstrap CIs and an explicit FP32 cuSPARSE correctness bound; results reported on two GPUs (RTX PRO 6000, H200) with multiple specialized-system baselines.

facts.title: SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering
facts.event_hint: SeDeM: a long-context QA framework that stores context as compressed hidden-state memory blocks, selects query-relevant blocks, and decompresses only those into a decoder layer, beating compression baselines and, with a 3B backbone, exceeding full-context fine-tuning on three of four datasets while lowering TTFT vs ICAE.
facts.problem: Long-context inference is costly: prefill self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length and the KV cache grows with processed tokens, while larger context windows do not guarantee reliable evidence use. Existing soft-compression methods use an LLM as compressor and rely on compact memory tokens both to preserve information and to condition the decoder, coupling storage and decoding.
facts.mechanism: SeDeM decouples compact memory storage from decoder conditioning. A frozen LLM extracts hidden states from a chosen intermediate Transformer layer; a lightweight compressor stores each segment as a memory block; a query-conditioned selector (trained with block-level evidence supervision) picks relevant blocks; a decompressor expands only the selected blocks into hidden states compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. The decoder thus avoids both full-context processing and direct generation from highly compressed slots. Because memory construction is query-independent, memories are reusable across queries and support cross-model (small encoder, larger decoder) use.

evidence.claim: On four long-context QA benchmarks SeDeM beats the evaluated compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-backbone settings; with the 3B backbone it exceeds full-context fine-tuning on three datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, QASPER, HotpotQA-Distractor).
evidence.value: 3B SeDeM > full-context FT on 3 of 4 datasets
evidence.baseline: LongLLMLingua, HMT, ICAE, 500x, Activation Beacon; full-context fine-tuning reference
evidence.condition: Llama-3.2-1B and 3B backbones, F1/ROUGE-L
evidence.source_locator: Table 2, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: Concrete 3B F1 scores: 2WikiMultiHopQA 67.25 (SeDeM) vs 62.50 (full-context FT) and 38.77 (ICAE); HotpotQA-Distractor 58.30 vs 36.73 (full-context FT); on MuSiQue SeDeM (21.85) remains below full-context FT (32.54).
evidence.condition: Llama-3.2-3B-Base
evidence.source_locator: Table 2, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: SeDeM reduces online time-to-first-token versus ICAE: averaged across the four datasets, 3B TTFT is 79.60 ms vs 195.76 ms (2.46x), and 1B TTFT is 46.56 ms vs 81.07 ms (1.74x); on QASPER 3B the speedup reaches 3.77x (96.50 ms vs 364.10 ms).
evidence.condition: Fully online protocol (includes compression, selection, decoder prefill)
evidence.source_locator: Table 3, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: SeDeM also improves autoregressive decoding throughput versus ICAE: 3B avg 45.16 vs 41.17 Tok/s (1.10x) and 1B avg 77.78 vs 71.82 Tok/s (1.08x); early-exit query encoding reduces 3B selection latency from ~26 ms to ~13 ms.
evidence.condition: Same backbones
evidence.source_locator: Table 3 and Section 6.2, PDF Page 7

evidence.claim: SeDeM's added inference-active modules are 33.59M params (2.72% of the frozen 1B backbone) and 75.55M params (2.35% of the 3B backbone), excluding LoRA adapters.
evidence.condition: Inference-time active modules
evidence.source_locator: Table 9, PDF Page 16

facts.evaluation_context: Four long-context QA benchmarks: 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, QASPER, HotpotQA-Distractor (train/val splits reported in Table 7). Backbones Llama-3.2-1B-Base and 3B-Base (frozen + LoRA). Baselines: LongLLMLingua (hard), HMT/ICAE/500x (soft), Activation Beacon (KV/activation), plus frozen and full-context fine-tuned references. Metrics: token-level F1 and ROUGE-L. Efficiency measured by TTFT (ms) and throughput (Tok/s) under a fully online protocol. A cross-model row uses a 1B encoder with a 3B decoder (e.g., HotpotQA F1 44.39).
facts.limitations: Explicitly stated by the authors: (1) the selector needs block-level evidence labels for training (all four benchmarks provide them); without labels, selector-disabled mode forgoes the efficiency gains of top-K selection. (2) Only Llama-3.2-1B and 3B are evaluated; transfer to substantially larger backbones is unverified. (3) Extraction and injection layers are chosen empirically, with no principled procedure for new backbone families. (4) With 3B, SeDeM stays below full-context FT on MuSiQue, and the selection budget K trades quality against context/efficiency. (5) Latency follows a fully online protocol; precomputing query-independent memories could improve efficiency but is not evaluated.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to compression/transfer/placement. SeDeM's query-independent memory construction makes compressed context reusable across multiple queries over the same context, and its selective decompression reduces both decode cost and TTFT. For cross-region or cross-session reuse, storing compact hidden-state memory blocks (rather than full KV) could lower bandwidth and storage cost while preserving QA quality, with the caveat that selection currently relies on evidence labels.
source_notes: All QA scores are from Table 2 and efficiency numbers from Table 3 (PDF Page 7).
Parameter-overhead figures are from Table 9 (PDF Page 16).
Limitations are transcribed from the explicit Limitations section (PDF Page 9).

facts.title: TokTier: Exact Stateful CPU+GPU Tokenization for Agentic LLM Serving
facts.event_hint: TokTier (ASU) introduces a stateful CPU+GPU tokenization service that guarantees byte-identical token IDs, cutting tokenization time so sharply that under a 50ms P99 objective 4 CPU cores + 1 GPU sustain 1,821 req/s where a 16-core stateless front end saturates at 40.
facts.problem: LLM serving stacks cache prompt KV state but the front end still re-tokenizes the full request text on every call. For coding agents that append a small tool result to a long transcript, tokenization grows from 10% to 64% of time-to-first-token as the fleet prompt-cache hit rate approaches 0.99, because a short append can shift token boundaries near the end of the prior sequence.
facts.mechanism: A two-mode stateful tokenization service enforcing one contract (emitted IDs always identical to full reference tokenization). For session continuations it keeps the prior token sequence, re-tokenizes a small window around the append, and splices only when a per-request check finds a stable pre-tokenization boundary (else widens or falls back). For calls without a reusable prefix it decomposes GPT-family regex pre-tokenization into run-local rules and runs exact pre-tokenization and BPE on a GPU. A sampled shadow verifier re-checks live traffic against the reference.

evidence.claim: Across 153,951 agent calls the median append is ~1.4K characters and only 1.0-3.6% of calls start or rebuild a session; at the fleet's 94.1% prompt-cache hit rate, as it approaches 0.99 tokenization grows from 10% to 64% of time to first token.
evidence.value: median append 1.4K chars; 1.0-3.6% session starts; tokenization 10%->64% of TTFT
evidence.condition: 153,951 calls from two agent ecosystems; component measurements at varying prompt-cache hit rates
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Abstract): 'Across 153,951 calls ... the median call appends only about 1.4 K characters, and only 1.0-3.6% of calls start or re-build a session ... the aggregate prompt-cache hit rate is 94.1%, and as it approaches 0.99, tokenization grows from 10% to 64% of time to first token.'

evidence.claim: Incremental repair takes 0.5-1.1ms from 100K to 3M characters, up to 437x faster than HF tokenization and 2.1x faster at 1M characters than Gigatoken (the strongest cache-based baseline) in its most favorable, fully prewarmed mode; GPU full tokenization encodes 1M characters in 0.87ms, up to 491x below HF and 23.4x below the fastest published CPU method.
evidence.value: repair 0.5-1.1ms (437x vs HF; 2.1x vs Gigatoken); GPU 0.87ms @1M (491x vs HF; 23.4x vs fastest CPU)
evidence.baseline: HuggingFace tokenization; Gigatoken (cache-based, fully prewarmed); fastest published CPU method
evidence.condition: 17 production tokenizer families; 1.5x10^10 split checks; 12.4TB real-text corpus; 93,000+ replayed agent steps; zero divergence
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Abstract): 'Incremental repair takes 0.5-1.1 ms from 100 K to 3 M characters, up to 437x faster than HF tokenization and 2.1x faster at 1 M characters than the strongest cache-based baseline (i.e., Gigatoken) ... GPU full tokenization encodes a 1 M-character request in 0.87 ms, up to 491x below HF tokenization and 23.4x below the fastest previously published CPU method.'

evidence.claim: With vLLM in the loop, TokTier lowers median time to first token by 16-34% in loaded regimes and P99 by 23% under recorded burst arrivals.
evidence.condition: Closed-loop sessions; e.g., 95K tokens/session improves median TTFT 23% with two back-to-back sessions, 16% with three, 34% with two sessions plus a two-second think time

evidence.claim: Under a 50ms P99 objective, four repair cores plus one GPU sustain 1,821 requests/s, where a 16-core stateless CPU front end saturates at 40.
evidence.value: 1,821 req/s (4 cores + 1 GPU) vs 40 req/s (16-core stateless)
evidence.condition: 50ms P99 TTFT objective
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Abstract): 'Under a 50 ms P99 objective, a four-core repair pool plus one GPU sustains 1,821 requests/s, where a 16-core stateless CPU front end saturates at 40.'

evidence.claim: Per-request CPU time is 13.4ms for fastokens vs 2.3ms for TokTier repair and 0.15ms for GPU full tokenization; at 0.5 req/s per inference GPU this is 6.7 / 1.1 / 0.1 front-end CPU cores per 1,000 GPUs. Session token state costs ~16 bytes/token (a 500K-token session holds <15MB) vs gigabytes for the corresponding KV state.
evidence.value: 13.4ms vs 2.3ms vs 0.15ms per request; 6.7/1.1/0.1 cores per 1,000 GPUs; <15MB for 500K-token session
evidence.condition: 153,529 calls with complete token accounting (mean 117K tokens, mean hit 0.88); rate normalization at 0.5 req/s per inference GPU
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 23 (Table 8) and PDF Page 14 (Section 5.7 Cost and resource use): '13.4 ms of CPU time per request for fastokens and 2.3 ms for TokTier repair ... GPU full tokenization contributes 0.15 ms ... 6.7, 1.1, and 0.1 front-end CPU cores per 1,000 GPUs ... a growing 500 K-token session holds its resident footprint under 15 MB.'

facts.evaluation_context: Workload: 153,951 calls from two agent ecosystems (SWE-smith streams under Qwen3, Llama 3.1, gpt-oss; plus public Codex trace). Hardware: GPU full tokenization benchmarked across RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000, GH200, H100 NVL, A100 (Table 9); repair measured with reference HF/Rust engines. Differential campaigns: 17 production tokenizer families, 1.5x10^10 split checks, 12.4TB real-text corpus, 93,000+ replayed agent steps, zero divergence. Closed-loop TTFT measured with vLLM at 95K tokens/session. Shadow verifier caught a history-dependent bug in a widely deployed production Rust tokenizer (39/40 sampled sessions diverged).
facts.limitations: At four concurrent sessions the inference engine cannot retain the needed KV state and prefix reuse collapses (tokenization placement becomes irrelevant). For large appends (delta=100K chars, beyond P99 of 38K / the 0.8% of calls reaching 50K) the fully prewarmed cache leads repair at every context shape; three explored prototype routes (A: parallel repair; B: cache-based window engine) are exploration prototypes that have not passed the certification battery gating the shipped repair path. GPU is only ~1.5x better in tokens/watt than the best 32-core CPU config under an accounting that favors the CPU.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to cross-region / agent-cache infrastructure: tokenization is an overlooked front-end bottleneck that dominates TTFT once KV-cache reuse is saturated. TokTier's exactness contract (byte-identical IDs, certified-boundary splice) is what makes incremental token-state reuse safe alongside prefix-cache and KV-cache reuse, and its small per-session state (<15MB vs gigabytes for KV) makes token-state sharing across regions far cheaper than KV-state sharing.
